The Backlog Is Not A Plan

Teodoro Vilas Jun 18, 2024

A backlog is a list of things nobody has said no to yet. That is a useful artefact and it is not a plan, and the difference matters most at exactly the moment a team starts treating the first as the second. A plan says what happens next and what that forecloses. A backlog says what has been thought of.

The tell is the ordering. In a plan, the order is a claim: this before that, because that depends on this, or because we would rather learn the first thing before committing to the second. In a backlog the order is an accident of when each item was typed, decorated afterwards with a priority field that everyone sets to the same value.

Where the confusion comes from

Nobody decides to confuse the two. It happens because the backlog is the only written thing, and a written thing attracts the questions a plan would answer. Someone asks what we are doing this quarter, the backlog is what exists, and the top of the backlog becomes the answer by default.

Once that has happened, the backlog stops being a place to put ideas. Adding to it now means arguing about the quarter, so people stop adding, and the one artefact that was genuinely useful quietly dies of being promoted.

What to do instead

Keep both, and keep them apart. The backlog stays unordered and cheap to add to; the plan is short, dated, and says what it rules out. I write mine as a paragraph rather than a list, because a paragraph cannot hide the fact that it has no argument in it, and a list can.

This is the part people push back on, usually by pointing at a newsletter somewhere that recommends the opposite. They may well be right for their team. What I am confident about is the diagnosis, not the prescription.
